title: Extract User Flows
bottom_line: Run this command in your app's project and Claude writes user-flows.md, a list of every way a person can use your app, each listed once.

sections.heading: Type the command, with two optional extras

blocks.caption: Both extras are optional and can come in any order.

blocks.title: What happens when you run it

nodes.label: You run the command
nodes.note: Inside your app's project folder in Claude Code.

nodes.label: Claude maps the app
nodes.note: Every flow is grounded in evidence from the code. It never invents features.

nodes.label: user-flows.md at root
nodes.note: Plus a short note in the project's CLAUDE.md.

blocks.title: The two optional extras
rows: Sets how comprehensive the list is: how many flows you get, not how detailed each one is.
Any other free text, such as "login", "checkout and payments" or "the admin panel"
Only flows for features matching that description are extracted. On an existing file, only that section is replaced; other sections and their IDs stay stable.

blocks.title: Examples
blocks.code:
/user-flows:extract-user-flows
/user-flows:extract-user-flows medium
/user-flows:extract-user-flows low checkout and payments
/user-flows:extract-user-flows login

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Nothing beyond Claude Code is needed. The skill reads the code and writes `user-flows.md`.
The plugin has no environment variables and no plugin settings.
Run it in the application's project folder, because it extracts flows from the app in the current working directory.

Typical reasons to use it: you want to extract, list, map or inventory the user flows, user journeys, usage scenarios or interaction paths of your app, especially before writing automated (E2E) tests.

sections.heading: A user flow is one complete thing a person does

blocks.text: A **user flow** is one complete, goal-directed interaction a client can have with the app, from where it starts to an outcome you can see. Another example: login, then search, then add to cart, then checkout.
Flows are the unit a later model turns into automated tests. So each flow must be testable on its own: concrete steps, a clear starting state and an outcome that can be checked.

terms.definition: One complete interaction a person has with the app, from entry point to an outcome you can observe.
How comprehensive the list is: low, medium or high.
A part of the app, such as Authentication. Flows are grouped under one heading per area.
A stable number such as UF-001 that tests use to point back at a flow.

sections.heading: Granularity decides how many flows you get

rows: Only the critical happy paths: one flow per major feature, the paths the business would notice breaking within an hour.
All happy paths plus the important variations: validation failures the user will commonly hit, alternate entry points, and cancel or back-out paths on destructive or paid actions.

Everything in medium plus edge cases, error and permission-denied paths, empty states and boundary behaviors such as an expired session, a double submit, or opening a protected page without logging in.
blocks.caption: Steps stay concrete at every level. Only the number of flows changes.

blocks.text: At `high`, the aim is the full set of flows a thorough QA engineer would list.

before.label: Duplicates
before.text: One flow per search term: each one has the same steps and the same outcome, and only the data value is different.

after.label: Merged
after.text: One flow: "search for any term", with the changing input noted.

blocks.caption: Flows that differ only in data values are merged into one.

blocks.text: A flow that is just the start of a longer flow only counts as its own flow if it ends in a different outcome that can be checked.

sections.heading: You get user-flows.md, with every flow in the same shape

blocks.title: The five lines of every flow

cards.title: Actor
cards.text: Who performs it, for example an anonymous user or an admin.

cards.title: Precondition
cards.text: The state needed before the flow starts, for example "registered account exists".

cards.title: Steps
cards.text: The actions, joined by arrows. Each step is one user action or visible change, concrete enough to automate, such as "click Purchase on the item page".

cards.title: Expected
cards.text: An outcome a test could check: a URL, visible text, a record created, an email queued. Never vague, like "it works".

cards.title: Source
cards.text: The key files or routes in the code that implement the flow.

blocks.title: The file's layout
blocks.code:
# User Flows

> granularity: <low|medium|high> | area: <filter or "all"> | generated: <YYYY-MM-DD>

## <Area name, e.g. Authentication>

### UF-001: <Short flow name>
- **Actor:** <who performs it, e.g. anonymous user, admin>
- **Precondition:** <required state before the flow, e.g. "registered account exists">
- **Steps:** <step 1> → <step 2> → <step 3>
- **Expected:** <observable, assertable outcome>
- **Source:** <key file(s)/route(s) implementing this flow>

blocks.title: Rules the file follows
items: IDs are numbered in order (`UF-001`, `UF-002`, and so on) across the whole file, and an ID is never reused for a different flow.
Flows are grouped under one heading per area, so a run limited to one area can replace that section cleanly.
Each step is a single user action or visible change, without implementation detail a test does not need.
The Expected line is always something a test can check.

blocks.title: Where the flows come from
blocks.text: Every flow is based on evidence in the code, never on features that do not exist. If the repository has a graphify knowledge graph (a `graphify-out/` folder) and the `/graphify` skill is available, Claude checks that first.

sections.heading: Running it again replaces the whole file or one area

blocks.text: With an area, numbering continues from the highest existing ID. That keeps the IDs your tests already refer to stable.

sections.heading: It also leaves a short note in your project's CLAUDE.md

cards.title: Where the list lives
cards.text: `user-flows.md` at the project root is the list of user flows, with stable `UF-NNN` IDs grouped by area, made by `/user-flows:extract-user-flows`.

cards.title: How to keep it current
cards.text: After behavior changes, use `/user-flows:update-user-flows`. Do not edit flow entries by hand, and never renumber IDs, because tests refer to them.

cards.title: How to get tests
cards.text: Playwright end-to-end (E2E) tests can be made and kept in sync from it with `/user-flows:test-user-flow`.

blocks.text: If `CLAUDE.md` does not exist, it is created with just this section. If the section is already there, it is refreshed rather than added a second time. It stays a few lines long.

sections.heading: This is the first step toward automated tests

blocks.title: What it reports when it finishes
items: The number of flows per area.
Whether CLAUDE.md was created or updated.
It does not paste the whole file back into the conversation.
